questions.topic_text: Topic 1.9: Refund of a government grant recognised as Deferred Grant Account and Profit and Loss, asset carrying amount unaffected
questions.why: Rank 36 topic (Refund of Government Grants); 81% match to an ICAI Study Material question; MTP September 2024 Set 2.
questions.question_html: Smile Ltd. purchased machinery for ₹80 lakhs (useful life 4 years and residual value ₹8 lakhs). Government grant received was ₹32 lakhs. The grant had to be refunded at the beginning of third year. Show the Journal Entry to be passed at the time of refund of grant and the value of the fixed assets in the third year and the amount of depreciation for remaining two years, if the grant had been credited to Deferred Grant A/c.
questions.answer_html:
As per AS 12 ‘Accounting for Government Grants’, income from a Deferred Grant Account is allocated to Profit and Loss usually over the periods and in the proportions in which depreciation on the related asset is charged. In the first two years, (₹32 lakhs/4 years) = ₹8 lakhs × 2 years = ₹16 lakhs is credited to P&L, leaving ₹16 lakhs as the balance of the Deferred Grant Account after two years. On refund of the grant:

AccountDr (₹ lakhs)Cr (₹ lakhs)
Deferred Grant A/c Dr.16
Profit & Loss A/c Dr.16
  To Bank A/c32
(Being Government grant refunded)

1. Value of fixed assets after two years but before refund of grant: initial cost ₹80 lakhs; depreciation per year = (₹80 lakhs − ₹8 lakhs)/4 years = ₹18 lakhs; book value after two years = 80 − (18×2) = ₹44 lakhs.

2. Value of fixed assets after refund of grant: on refund the Deferred Grant Account balance becomes nil, but the fixed asset continues to be shown in the books at ₹44 lakhs (unchanged — the refund does not restate the asset's carrying amount).

3. Depreciation for remaining two years: continues to be charged at ₹18 lakhs per annum for the remaining two years.
questions.mistake_text: Author’s Note: A common error here is restating the fixed asset's carrying amount upward on refund of the grant, rather than recognising that the refund is charged to the Deferred Grant Account balance and Profit and Loss, leaving the asset's carrying amount unaffected.

questions.topic_text: Topic 1.6/1.9: Grant deducted from a fixed asset's cost, and prospective adjustment of depreciation over the remaining useful life on partial refund of the grant

questions.topic_text: Topic 1.6: Depreciation impact of the asset-deduction, deferred-income and promoter's-contribution presentation methods, including a mid-life grant refund

topics.topic_name: Presentation of Grants Related to Specific Fixed Assets

questions.why: Rank 35 topic (Presentation of Grants Related to Specific Fixed Assets); MTP September 2025 Set 2.
questions.question_html: On 1st April 2023, Eleanor Limited purchased a manufacturing Plant for ₹60 lakhs, which has an estimated useful life of 10 years with a salvage value of ₹10 lakhs. On purchase of the Plant, a grant of ₹20 lakhs was received from the government. You are required to calculate the amount of depreciation as per AS 12 for the financial year 2024-25 in the following cases: (i) If the grant amount is deducted from the value of Plant. (ii) If the grant is treated as deferred income. (iii) If the grant amount is deducted from the value of Plant, but at the end of the year 2024-2025 grant is refunded to the extent of ₹4 lakhs, due to non-compliance of certain conditions. (iv) If the grant is treated as the promoter's contribution. (Assume depreciation on the basis of Straight-Line Method.)
questions.answer_html:
(i) If the grant amount is deducted from the value of Plant, depreciation = (₹60,00,000 − ₹10,00,000 − ₹20,00,000) ÷ 10 years = ₹3,00,000 p.a.

(ii) If the grant is treated as deferred income, depreciation = (₹60,00,000 − ₹10,00,000) ÷ 10 years = ₹5,00,000 p.a.

(iii) If the grant amount is deducted from the value of Plant, but at the end of the year 2024-25 grant is refunded to the extent of ₹4 lakh: depreciation for year 2023-24 remains (₹60,00,000 − ₹10,00,000 − ₹20,00,000) ÷ 10 years = ₹3,00,000; for the year 2024-25, depreciation = (₹60,00,000 − ₹10,00,000 − ₹20,00,000 − ₹3,00,000) ÷ 9 years = ₹3,00,000.

Note: It is assumed that the depreciation for the year has been charged on the book value of the plant before making adjustment for the grant refund. Alternatively, if depreciation is charged after making adjustment for the grant refund, depreciation for 2024-25 will be (₹60,00,000 − ₹10,00,000 − ₹20,00,000 + ₹4,00,000 − ₹3,00,000) ÷ 9 years = ₹3,44,444.

(iv) If the grant is treated as the promoter's contribution, depreciation = (₹60,00,000 − ₹10,00,000) ÷ 10 years = ₹5,00,000 p.a.
questions.mistake_text: Author’s Note: A common error here is treating the partial grant refund in case (iii) as a fresh transaction requiring the original 10-year schedule to be unwound, rather than simply adding the refunded amount back to the asset's remaining book value and re-spreading it over the remaining useful life.

questions.topic_text: Topic 1.9: Refund of a government grant related to a specific fixed asset increases the asset's book value, depreciated prospectively
questions.why: Rank 36 topic (Refund of Government Grants); MTP May 2023 Set 2.
questions.question_html: Caseworker Limited received a specific grant of ₹6 crore for acquiring the plant of ₹30 crore on 1.4.2016 having useful life of 10 years. At the beginning of the financial year 2021-2022, due to non-compliance of conditions laid down for the grant of ₹6 crore, the company had to refund the grant to the Government. What should be the treatment of the refund if grant was deducted from the cost of the plant during financial year 2016-2017? Assume depreciation is charged on fixed assets as per Straight Line Method.
questions.answer_html:
As per AS 12, the amount refundable in respect of grant related to specific fixed assets should be recorded by increasing the book value of the asset or by reducing the capital reserve or the deferred income balance, as appropriate, by the amount refundable. Where the book value of the asset is increased, depreciation on the revised book value should be provided prospectively over the residual useful life of the asset.

Where grant was deducted from the cost of the asset, initial value of the plant after deduction of grant amount of ₹6 crore would have been = ₹30 crore − ₹6 crore = ₹24 crore.

Carrying value of the plant after 5 years on 1.4.2021 = [(₹24 crore / 10 years) × 5 years] = ₹12 crore.

Annual depreciation charge would be ₹2.4 crore.

On refund of grant to the Government, the book value of the plant shall be increased by ₹6 crore i.e. ₹12 crore + ₹6 crore = ₹18 crore. The increased cost of ₹18 crore of the plant should be amortised prospectively over remaining 5 years of useful residual life. Depreciation charge in the year 2021-2022 would be ₹18 crore / 5 years = ₹3.6 crore instead of earlier ₹2.4 crore.
questions.mistake_text: Author’s Note: A common error is reversing the refund entry against the original grant-deduction entry retrospectively (restating prior years), rather than increasing the asset's current book value prospectively and depreciating the revised amount only over the remaining useful life.

questions.topic_text: Topic 1.8: Grants in the nature of promoters' contribution credited to Capital Reserve, never treated as revenue/deferred income

topics.topic_name: Presentation of Grants of the Nature of Promoters' Contribution

questions.why: Rank 368 topic (Presentation of Grants of the Nature of Promoters' Contribution); 58% match to an ICAI Study Material question; RTP May 2025.
questions.question_html: XYZ Limited has set-up its business in a designated backward area which entitles the company to receive from the Government of India a subsidy of 20% of the cost of investment. Having fulfilled all the conditions under the scheme, the company on its investment of ₹75 crore received ₹15 crore as subsidy from the Government in January 2024. The company wants to treat this receipt as an item of revenue and thereby reduce the losses for the year ended on 31st March, 2024. Keeping in view the relevant Accounting Standard, examine whether this action is justified or not.
questions.answer_html:
As per para 10 of AS 12 'Accounting for Government Grants', where government grants are in the nature of promoters' contribution – i.e. they are given with reference to the total investment in an undertaking, or by way of contribution towards its total capital outlay, and no repayment is ordinarily expected in respect thereof – the grants are treated as Capital Reserve, which can be neither distributed as dividend nor considered as deferred income.

In the given case, the subsidy received (20% of the cost of investment) is neither in relation to a specific fixed asset nor in relation to revenue – it is linked to the total investment made in the backward-area undertaking. It is therefore inappropriate to recognise this government grant in the profit and loss statement, since it is not earned but represents an incentive provided by the government without related costs.

The correct treatment is to credit the ₹15 crore subsidy to Capital Reserve. Therefore, the accounting treatment (treating it as revenue to reduce the reported loss) followed by the company is not proper.
questions.mistake_text: Author’s Note: A common error is treating any cash subsidy received as revenue income by default, without first testing whether it meets AS 12's specific "promoters' contribution" characterisation (tied to total investment, not a specific asset or specific revenue item), which mandates Capital Reserve treatment instead.

questions.topic_text: Topic 1.7: Refund of a grant previously deducted from asset cost - added back to the asset's carrying amount

topics.topic_name: Presentation of Grants Related to Revenue

questions.why: Rank 367 topic (Presentation of Grants Related to Revenue); RTP January 2026.
questions.question_html: Mediwell Hospitals Ltd. acquired 40 Doppler Scan Machines from Holiver Inc., USA, at US$1,65,100/unit at the start of FY2022-23, exchange rate ₹50/US$. Partly financed by a government grant of ₹5 crores (specific condition: refund on change in management/ownership control). In April 2025, 51% shareholding acquired by an overseas investor — management control changed, grant refund now due. Useful life 5 years, SLM at 20% p.a. Also: Bank charges US$4,000 (whole import), Sea freight ₹7,500/unit. No Capital Reserve or Deferred Income Account was maintained for the grant. Advise the accounting treatment for the grant refund per AS 12.
questions.answer_html:
The grant was received towards a fixed asset; the capital (deduction-from-cost) approach was adopted (confirmed by the absence of a Capital Reserve or Deferred Income Account).

Cost of asset (1,65,100 × 40 units × ₹50)3,302 lakhs
Add: Freight and other charges (4,000×50 bank charges + 7,500×40 sea freight)5 lakhs
Total cost3,307 lakhs
Less: Grant received(500 lakhs)
Cost as per AS 10 (net of grant)2,807 lakhs
Less: Depreciation for 3 years (2,807 × 20% × 3)(1,684.2 lakhs)
Carrying amount as on 1.4.2025 (before refund)1,122.8 lakhs
Add: Grant refunded500 lakhs
Revised carrying amount1,622.8 lakhs

Per AS 12, when a grant that was deducted from an asset's cost becomes refundable, the amount refundable is added back to the carrying amount of the asset (or the gross book value increased), rather than expensed — increasing the future depreciation charge over the asset's remaining life.
questions.mistake_text: Author’s Note: Some examinees expensed the refunded grant amount directly to the P&L, not applying AS 12's specific rule that a refund of a grant deducted from asset cost is added back to the carrying amount of that asset.

questions.topic_text: Topic 1.3: Revenue grants credited to P&L (or netted against the related expense)
questions.why: Rank 364 topic (Accounting Treatment of Government Grants); RTP September 2025.
questions.question_html: Zenith Industries Ltd. received ₹65 lakhs from a local authority to develop medical facilities for employees at its new township. Explain the accounting treatment per AS 12.
questions.answer_html: This is a grant in the nature of a revenue grant (related to employee welfare expenditure, not a specific fixed asset). Such grants are generally presented as a credit in the Statement of Profit and Loss, either separately or under "Other Income." Alternatively, the ₹65 lakhs may be deducted from the related expense (employee benefit expenses) instead.
questions.mistake_text: Author’s Note: Some examinees treated this as a capital grant since it funds facilities at a "newly built" site, missing that the grant's purpose (employee welfare) rather than the site's newness determines its revenue-grant classification.

questions.topic_text: Topic 1.8: Promoters'-contribution grants credited to Capital Reserve
questions.why: Rank 364 topic (Accounting Treatment of Government Grants); RTP September 2025.
questions.question_html: Zenith Industries Ltd. also received ₹82 lakhs as a Central Government subsidy for establishing a new production unit in a notified backward area, classified as being in the nature of promoters' contribution, intended to support long-term development. Explain the treatment per AS 12.
questions.answer_html: Per AS 12, grants in the nature of promoters' contribution — given with reference to total investment/capital outlay, with no repayment ordinarily expected — are treated as Capital Reserve, which can neither be distributed as dividend nor treated as deferred income. Since this ₹82 lakh subsidy is neither tied to a specific fixed asset nor to revenue, the full amount should be credited to Capital Reserve.
questions.mistake_text: Author’s Note: Some examinees treated this as deferred income to be amortised, not recognising the promoters'-contribution characterisation that requires direct Capital Reserve treatment.

questions.topic_text: Topic 1.4: Recognition of a government grant requires reasonable assurance of both compliance and receipt - mere application is insufficient
questions.why: Rank 365 topic (Recognition of Government Grants); RTP September 2024.
questions.question_html:
Energy Ltd. has acquired a generator on 1.4.2023 for ₹100 lakh. On 2.4.2023, it applied to Indian Renewal Energy Development Authority (IREDA) for a subsidy. The subsidy was granted in June, 2024 after the accounts for 2023-2024 were finalized. The company has not accounted for the subsidy for the year ended 31.3.2024.

State

  1. Is this a prior period item?
  2. How should the subsidy be accounted in the accounting year 2024-2025?
questions.answer_html:
The answer is in para 13 of AS 12 "Accounting for Government Grants" which permits recognition of grant only when there is reasonable assurance that –

  1. the enterprise will comply with the conditions attached to them and
  2. the subsidy will be received.

Mere making of an application does not provide the reasonable assurance that the subsidy will be received. Letter of sanction from IREDA is required to provide this assurance. Since, the subsidy was granted in June, 2024 after approval of accounts, non-recognition of grant in 2023-2024 will not be considered as an error. Hence, this is not a prior period item. Therefore, the company was right in not recognizing the grant.

Further, AS 4 requires adjustment of events occurring after the balance sheet date only upto the date of approval of accounts by the Board of Directors. In view of this, the company is correct in not adjusting the same in the accounts in the year 2023-2024.

(ii) The subsidy should be deducted from the cost of the generator. The revised unamortised amount of generator should be written off over the remaining useful life.

Alternatively, the same may be treated as ‘deferred income’ and allocated over the remaining useful life in the proportion in which depreciation is charged.
questions.mistake_text: Author’s Note: A common error is treating the mere filing of a subsidy application as sufficient grounds to recognize the grant, or alternatively treating the later grant of the subsidy as a prior period item requiring restatement of the already-approved 2023-2024 accounts.
